options.A: Which plan will look neater in my report to the area manager?
options.B: Which plan makes the customer's outcome more certain?
options.C: Which plan is easier for the team to run on the day?
options.D: Which plan would head office prefer to see on the floor?

questions.stem:
A customer comes to the till angry. His sofa was delivered damaged, and this is his third visit about it. He says, "Do something."
What is the best response?

options.A: "Three visits and a damaged sofa: you're right to be angry. I'm booking a replacement now and will call you Wednesday by noon."
options.B: "Damage has to be reported within two days. Let me check whether you did that."
options.C: "I'll sort everything out: a replacement, a full refund and a voucher, all today, no problem."
options.D: "I understand it's frustrating, but delays happen with every delivery, and it is not unusual."

questions.stem:
A new manager drafts a 30-day plan with five priorities. One reads: "Improve stock accuracy. Owner: the store. Check: end of month."
What is the best fix?

options.A: Keep all five, because a full month is long enough to make progress on every area.
options.B: Leave the line as it is, and share it with the team out loud rather than in writing.
options.C: Cut to no more than three, and give the stock line a measurable goal, a named owner and one behavior.
options.D: Keep five, but write each one in fewer words so that the whole plan reads quickly.

questions.stem:
Your 30-day plan has conversion as a priority, with a goal of 20 percent. At day 25 it is at 17. In the middle of the month, head office changed the price of your top-selling line. Your manager asks for an update.
Which update is best?

options.A: "We would have hit 20 percent by now, but head office changed the price of our top-selling line in the middle of the month."
options.B: "It may well recover on its own once customers get used to the new price, so I'll report when it does."
options.C: "The team has worked very hard in a month when the price change made the goal unrealistic for everyone."
options.D: "Conversion is 17 against 20. The price change was outside my control; what I own is our response, a greeting question at that aisle. I recommend we review the goal. I need your decision by Friday."

questions.stem:
Rana wants to know whether her listening and her matching of offers to needs are improving week by week.
Which number should she watch most closely?

options.A: Calls made, because more dials in a week show more effort and more chances taken.
options.B: Contact rate, because it shows how often her dials actually reach a person.
options.C: Average order value, because bigger orders always mean she listened better.
options.D: Conversion: the share of real conversations that end in the outcome.

questions.stem:
Karim's conversion is the best on the team, but his average order value is the lowest. Several of his customers call back within a month to move to a bigger plan.
What does this most likely tell you?

options.A: He should make more dials, because volume is what is holding his numbers back.
options.B: He is often recommending less than the customer really needs.
options.C: His contact rate must be low, so he keeps reaching the wrong people.
options.D: Nothing important, since conversion is the only number that reflects skill.

questions.stem:
Before a one-hour session, a rep writes her goal at the top of the page.
Which is the best session goal?

options.A: "Make as many calls as I can before five o'clock."
options.B: "Get through all 40 names on today's list."
options.C: "Book two meetings with small business owners."
options.D: "Sell harder than yesterday and close more deals."

questions.stem:
Omar calls a past customer whose broadband contract with his company ends this month. The customer is on an approved list.
Which opening is best?

options.A: "Hello, this is Omar from Brightwave. I know this call is unexpected, so if now is a bad time, just say so. I'm calling because your contract with us ends this month. How has the connection been for you lately?"
options.B: "Hi, how are you today? I'll be quick. I'm Omar from Brightwave, and we have a great deal I think you'll love. Have you got a minute to hear it?"
options.C: "Hello, Omar from Brightwave. Your contract ends this month, and we have some new plans. Would you like to hear about them now?"
options.D: "Hello, this is Omar from Brightwave. If now is a bad time, just say. Everyone on your street is switching to our new plan, so I wanted to make sure you don't miss out."

questions.stem:
You end your opener with an open question, and the line goes quiet for a couple of seconds.
What should you do?

options.A: Answer your own question, so the silence does not start to feel awkward.
options.B: Wait. The pause is space for the other person to think.
options.C: Fill the gap with the main benefits of the offer while you have their attention.
options.D: Ask, "Are you still there?" and repeat the whole opener a little faster.

questions.stem:
A woman calls the mobile line and says she wants to add a second SIM for her teenage son. On your screen you can see a family bundle, a TV add-on and phone insurance.
What is the best next step?

options.A: Mention the family bundle, the TV add-on and the insurance, so she knows everything you offer.
options.B: Read her the current promotion first, since it may change what she wants today.
options.C: Ask for her name again and run through the full standard script before anything else.
options.D: Ask a little about how her son will use the phone, and understand that first.

questions.stem:
A shop owner says, "Not a good time." You give one calm line with your true reason and offer to let her go. She says, "Really, not now."
What do you do?

options.A: Thank her and close honestly, offering to call at a time that suits her.
options.B: Read out the main points of the offer quickly, before she has a chance to hang up.
options.C: Tell her it will only take a minute, so that she stays on the line a little longer.
options.D: Make the same push a third time, more slowly, so that she finally hears your reason.

questions.stem:
After your opener, a small business owner says, "Honestly, our deliveries are a mess every Monday."
What is the best next move?

options.A: Now that there is interest, explain your delivery service and its main features in full.
options.B: Ask four quick questions in a row about volume, drivers, routes and costs.
options.C: Say back what you heard in a few words, ask one short open question, then stop.
options.D: Say, "So you're busy on Mondays. Would our delivery service help with that?"

questions.stem:
A client says, "We lose half a morning chasing unpaid invoices."
What should your note say?

options.A: "lose half a morning chasing unpaid invoices"
options.B: "invoicing inefficiency"
options.C: "busy mornings"
options.D: "interested in product"

questions.stem:
You want a sense of a small firm's budget without making the owner defensive.
Which question fits the course?

options.A: "What is your budget for this?"
options.B: "How much are you willing to spend each month?"
options.C: "Most firms your size choose between a smaller starting option and a fuller one. Which sounds more like you?"
options.D: "Our plans start at 90 a month. Can you afford that?"

questions.stem:
On a phone call, a rep reads out all four plans in detail. The client says, "Let me think about it."
What is the most likely reason?

options.A: The client is not interested and is ending the call politely.
options.B: The price of every plan is too high for the client's budget.
options.C: The client needs to hear about more plans before deciding.
options.D: Too many options with nothing to look at stalled the decision.

questions.stem:
Earlier in the call, the client said, "I'm sick of the system crashing every Friday." Now she says, "Another company quoted us less."
What is the best response?

options.A: "I understand, but our servers are faster and our support team runs around the clock."
options.B: (pause) "That's fair. Price matters. The question I'd ask is what those Friday crashes cost you now. What would need to be true for this to be worth it?"
options.C: "I can take ten percent off if you sign today, so that we beat their quote."
options.D: "That's fair, price matters. So would you like to go ahead with us anyway?"

questions.stem:
A client says, "That's a lot." The rep stays quiet for two slow breaths, and the client adds, "Our last provider promised the same and let us down."
What did the pause do?

options.A: It made the client uncomfortable, which pressured him into talking.
options.B: It gave the rep time to prepare a full list of features to answer with.
options.C: It gave the client room to say the real reason behind the objection.
options.D: It signalled doubt, so the client tried to reassure the rep.

questions.stem:
You are allowed to waive the setup fee. A client asks, "Can you do something on the price?"
What do you do?

options.A: Offer to waive the fee in return for something of equal value, such as a twelve-month term.
options.B: Waive the fee straight away as a goodwill gesture, so the client feels looked after.
options.C: Promise a bigger discount on the call and get it approved by your manager afterwards.
options.D: Say "I'm sure we can do something" and work out the details after the call.

questions.stem:
A rep listens to her recorded calls. Every Acknowledge she uses is the same two words: "I understand."
What should she change?

options.A: Add "but" and a short explanation, so the acknowledgment leads somewhere useful.
options.B: Use a sentence she would actually say, such as "That's a fair worry."
options.C: Drop the acknowledgment and go straight to the reframe to save time on each call.
options.D: Say "I understand" twice, so it sounds warmer and more sincere to the client.

questions.stem:
You ran A.R.T. on a client's concern, and she says, "OK, that makes sense." You know her criteria, and the fit is clear.
What is the best next move?

options.A: "Great. Shall I send the contract over now?"
options.B: Keep reframing for another minute, to be sure the concern is fully gone.
options.C: Tell her the offer ends today, so she decides before the call ends.
options.D: Restate her criteria, show the evidence, name the consequence honestly, ask an open question, then offer two real dates.

questions.stem:
A client's current contract charges an exit fee if she leaves before March. It is January.
Which Consequence line is honest?

options.A: "Switching now means paying the exit fee. Waiting until March costs you nothing, so starting then may suit you better."
options.B: "Waiting is risky. Prices may go up next week, so it's better to switch today."
options.C: Skip the Consequence step, since mentioning the fee could lose the sale.
options.D: "Most of your neighbours have already switched, so waiting makes no sense."

questions.stem:
A call ends with the office manager saying, "We decide after the budget meeting on the 14th. Call me the next day at ten."
Which log entry is best?

options.A: "Interested. Call back."
options.B: "Office manager, positive call, good chance."
options.C: "Follow up after their meeting sometime next week."
options.D: "Spoke to Lina (office manager). Said: 'We decide after the budget meeting on the 14th.' Agreed: call on the 15th at 10:00."

questions.stem:
After fifteen fast "no"s in a row, a rep starts to feel the session is a failure and that the problem is her.
What does the course recommend?

options.A: Push harder on the next calls to make up for the ones she lost.
options.B: Treat each outcome as information and score herself on what she controls.
options.C: Stop logging the quick no's, so the session feels less discouraging.
options.D: Judge the session only by sales, since that is the number that really matters.

questions.stem:
In his second week in a new tele sales job, Ali wants to impress his manager. He plans to double his dials before learning the product or the rules on who may be called and when.
What should he do instead?

options.A: Double the dials anyway, because a high call count shows effort and effort is what counts.
options.B: Skip logging the short calls, so he has more time in each session to dial.
options.C: Learn the product and the contact rules first, keep his own call log, and watch conversations and conversion, not dials alone.
options.D: Extend his calls into the evening, when more people are home, to raise his contact rate.

questions.stem:
A new area manager writes down what she owns.
Which item is hers, not her unit managers'?

options.A: Which priorities matter across the area, and how her support is spread.
options.B: The daily decisions on each unit's pipeline and which quotes to chase first.
options.C: Each branch's customer relationships and who calls which client this week.
options.D: The daily behavior of each team on the sales floor and on the phones.

questions.stem:
An area manager wants all four units to open client calls with the same three-sentence script, and to reply to every new enquiry within the same set time.
What should become an area standard?

options.A: Both, because consistency across units always builds client trust.
options.B: Neither, because each unit manager knows their own clients best.
options.C: The response time, while the call opening stays with each unit.
options.D: The script, because the wording is what clients hear first on every call.

questions.stem:
On a call, a unit manager tells you, "Clients are unhappy everywhere this month." She bases it on one difficult conversation she had yesterday.
How should you treat it on your area map?

options.A: Rank her unit first for support straight away, since she raised the alarm.
options.B: As a lead to check against evidence, such as response times, missed promises and what clients said.
options.C: Ignore it completely, because one manager's feelings are not data.
options.D: Move most of your support to her unit until the mood there improves.

questions.stem:
One unit's conversion has slipped for two months. You are tempted to sit in on its pipeline review and phone the stalled clients yourself.
What is the best approach?

options.A: Phone the stalled clients yourself, since a senior voice reassures them and wins back time.
options.B: Set the unit a conversion push for next month, so the manager knows it is a priority.
options.C: Tell the manager how to close each stalled deal, since you have more selling experience.
options.D: Compare the slip with lead quality and cycle, take questions to the manager, and agree one action she owns.

questions.stem:
Unit North had 400 qualified opportunities and closed 80. Unit South had 100 and closed 30.
Which unit converted better?

options.A: North, because it closed far more sales over the period.
options.B: They converted equally well over the period.
options.C: Neither can be judged, because the units are different sizes.
options.D: South, at 30 percent against North's 20 percent.

questions.stem:
Before discussing any unit's performance, you use the course's fixed routine.
Which order is correct?

options.A: What changed, who is different, which behavior drives it, one thing to try.
options.B: Who is different, what changed, one thing to try, which behavior drives it.
options.C: Which behavior drives it, what changed, who is different, one thing to try.
options.D: One thing to try, what changed, which behavior drives it, who is different.

questions.stem:
After five steady months, one unit's conversion fell this month. A colleague says, "That manager has lost the plot."
What do you do first?

options.A: Call the manager and tell her the unit is now underperforming.
options.B: Set a recovery target for next month and review it then.
options.C: Set the drop beside lead quality, cycle, capacity and mix for the same periods.
options.D: Compare its closed totals with the largest unit in the area.

questions.stem:
Your comparison shows one unit's follow-up rate dropped from 85 to 55 percent in a month. You meet the unit manager.
What is the best opening?

options.A: "Your team has gone lazy on follow-up, and I need it fixed this month."
options.B: "Follow-up dropped from 85 to 55 percent. What changed? Pick one opportunity that went cold and walk me through it." Then wait.
options.C: "I'll sit with your reps this week and coach them on follow-up myself."
options.D: "Here are five things to fix: scripts, timing, CRM use, reminders and weekly checks."

questions.stem:
You observe a unit manager coaching a rep after a lost deal.
What should your feedback focus on?

options.A: The rep's selling mistakes, which you explain to the rep directly afterwards.
options.B: The manager's personality and general style as a leader of the team.
options.C: The manager's coaching behavior in that session.
options.D: The unit's conversion figures for the month so far.

questions.stem:
This morning you watched unit manager Lina coach a rep, Omar. Three times she finished his answers for him.
Which feedback follows SBI with the practice step?

options.A: "Lina, you are too controlling in your coaching sessions."
options.B: "Lina, in this morning's session you interrupted Omar three times. Try not to do that."
options.C: "Lina, you were impatient this morning, and Omar seemed unhappy."
options.D: "Lina, this morning you finished Omar's answers three times, and he stopped offering ideas. Let's rehearse letting him finish."

questions.stem:
A unit manager's coaching log shows nine sessions this month. Eight were with the same top rep.
What do you do?

options.A: Point to the pattern and ask how coaching will reach the rest of the team, with a dated check.
options.B: Praise the number of sessions, since nine is well above the area average.
options.C: Coach the other reps yourself, so nobody on the team is left behind.
options.D: Leave it alone, because the top rep's numbers went up this month.

questions.stem:
A unit manager tells you her lost deals are "all about price." The reps wrote "price" in the lost-sale notes, but the clients' own words say, "I didn't understand what was included." Other units do not show this.
What is your best move?

options.A: Approve a lower price for that unit, since the manager knows her clients best.
options.B: Read the clients' words with her, ask her to walk you through one lost deal, then agree one coaching change.
options.C: Accept the reps' summaries, since they were the ones on the calls.
options.D: Roll out new pricing materials to every unit in the area.

questions.stem:
Two responses could both fix a problem: a short shared product explanation, or a full redesign of all materials.
What should you do first?

options.A: The full redesign, because it covers everything at once.
options.B: The smaller response, tested first in a limited pilot.
options.C: Both at the same time, so the problem disappears faster.
options.D: Neither, until the problem appears in every single unit.

questions.stem:
Clients in four units say, "I couldn't tell which package was right for me." Each unit compares the offer to a different benchmark.
Which response fits?

options.A: Coach each manager separately on how their own team explains packages.
options.B: Ask every unit to make more calls this month to make up the gap.
options.C: Lower prices, so the choice feels less risky to the client.
options.D: One shared comparison guide that every unit uses.

questions.stem:
A month after rolling out a practice to three units, every manager tells you, "Yes, we're doing it."
What do you do next?

options.A: Check conversations, notes and observations for real use, against the measure set before the pilot.
options.B: Take their word for it, since they own execution in their units.
options.C: Wait for the quarter's results before looking at anything.
options.D: Roll it out to the remaining units straight away.

questions.stem:
Your two-unit pilot has ended. In one unit the success measure was met. In the other it was partly met, because the manager started two weeks late.
How does it go in your area review?

options.A: Report the unit that met the measure, and leave the other out to keep the story clear.
options.B: Announce an area-wide rollout now, since the pilot has proved that it works.
options.C: Mark one done and one partial with the reason, and recommend the next step with a date.
options.D: Leave the pilot out of the review until both units have complete results.

questions.stem:
Your draft area review is nine pages of unit-by-unit detail.
What should it contain instead?

options.A: All nine pages, so the leader has every fact available.
options.B: One line: "Sales are down, we are working on it."
options.C: A story of the month's main client conversations.
options.D: Results against target with context, customer-facing risks, and decisions needed.

questions.stem:
You hold a quarterly area review and send nothing in between. Your senior leader has started skipping your updates.
What does the course recommend?

options.A: Wait for the next review and make it longer and more detailed.
options.B: A short written summary after each review, updates at an agreed interval, and a note when a commitment closes.
options.C: A long daily report covering every unit in the area.
options.D: Contact the leader only when there is bad news to share.

questions.stem:
Your unit managers report twelve client concerns this month.
Which belong in your review to senior leaders?

options.A: All twelve, so that nothing important is missed.
options.B: None, because client concerns belong to unit managers.
options.C: Only those that would change a senior leader's decision.
options.D: The ones raised by the loudest or most senior clients.

questions.stem:
A key account shared by two units complains that each unit gives a different turnaround time for repairs. Fixing it needs a senior decision on one area-wide repair promise. The account manager in one unit leads the client relationship.
What do you do?

options.A: In the review, name the risk with evidence from both units, note that the account manager leads the client, and recommend one standard with a decision date.
options.B: Call the client yourself and promise one turnaround time, then tell the two managers.
options.C: Send senior leaders every unit's repair figures and let them draw their own conclusions.
options.D: Ask senior leaders in the review, "What should we do about repair times?"

questions.stem:
On her first Monday as sales manager, Hana sits down to plan the week.
Which question should she start with?

options.A: "What do I need to close personally this week to hit my number?"
options.B: "Where should our selling effort go this cycle, and what will it cost?"
options.C: "Which accounts called me most last week, so I can get back to them first?"
options.D: "Which of the biggest deals can I take over myself to make sure they land?"

questions.stem:
The business objective is growth this year. Segment one, hospitals, is large, but you have no references there and buying runs through nine-month tenders. Segment two, small clinics, is smaller, but your team already has 30 relationships there and clinics buy direct.
Which should be the priority this cycle?

options.A: Hospitals, because the bigger market is the bigger forecast.
options.B: Both equally, so no opportunity is missed this year.
options.C: Neither, until the team has sold in both for a full year.
options.D: Clinics, because the team can serve them well now.

questions.stem:
A draft priority plan says, "We will stop field visits to our smallest accounts this cycle." Nothing else is written about those accounts.
What is missing?

options.A: How those accounts will be served instead, such as inside support or a partner.
options.B: Nothing, because the not-pursued line is already the hardest part to write.
options.C: A promise to keep visiting them now and then, so nobody notices the change.
options.D: A few more priorities, so the plan looks as ambitious as the business wants.

questions.stem:
Your plan frees two reps from core accounts to work a new segment. When you allocate the target, the core channel's slice is still the same as last year.
What should you do?

options.A: Keep the core slice as it is and expect the remaining reps to cover the freed reps' accounts too.
options.B: Raise the new segment's slice until the totals match, because the business needs the growth.
options.C: Lower the core slice for the capacity moved, write the trade-off beside it, and raise any gap in the total openly.
options.D: Quietly drop the new segment if it falls behind, so the core slice can still be met.

questions.stem:
You are setting next year's target for one channel.
Which is the right base to start from?

options.A: What it actually delivered over the last few comparable periods.
options.B: Its single best month this year, multiplied by twelve.
options.C: Last year's total plus a growth percentage that sounds inspiring.
options.D: The growth rate your main competitor announced this year.

questions.stem:
A company sells through distributors and through a direct key-account team. The new manager splits the target equally across four regions, because that is how the org chart is drawn.
What does the course say?

options.A: Keep the regional split, since equal slices feel fair to every team.
options.B: Split it evenly by rep headcount, so every person carries the same number.
options.C: Split by channel first, then by territory inside each channel.
options.D: Keep one shared number for the whole team, so everyone owns all of it.

questions.stem:
A manager's allocation adds exactly 10 percent to each channel's slice from last year. The total is last year's plus 10 percent.
What check does the course ask for?

options.A: None, because a proportional increase is the fairest split there is.
options.B: Build the allocation bottom-up from channel evidence and capacity, then compare.
options.C: Raise the strongest channel's slice further, to build in a safety margin.
options.D: Leave it, and let the review points correct any slice that turns out wrong.

questions.stem:
At the planned mid-year review point, the partner channel is 30 percent ahead of its slice. Most of the gain comes from one large order. A team lead proposes moving part of the direct target onto partners for the rest of the year.
What do you do?

options.A: Agree now, since the partner channel has clearly outgrown its slice.
options.B: Raise the partner slice and keep direct unchanged, so the total rises.
options.C: Change nothing, and wait for the year-end result before looking again.
options.D: Strip out the one-off order, check the written partner assumption, then decide what the review may change.

questions.stem:
Calls made dropped sharply this month, but closed deals are on plan.
What is the most likely reading?

options.A: There is no problem, because the outcome numbers are steady.
options.B: Activity does not matter, because outcomes held without it.
options.C: The team must have changed size, so the averages moved.
options.D: A lag effect: the drop may show up in closed deals later.

questions.stem:
Your pipeline shows few deals at first contact, and fourteen deals that have sat in negotiation for more than three months.
How should you read it?

options.A: As a warning: deals sitting still late in the pipeline may not be real deals.
options.B: As a healthy pipeline, since a full late stage means a strong quarter is coming.
options.C: As a problem at first contact only, because the early stage is too thin.
options.D: As forecast-ready, so add all fourteen to the forecast at full value.

questions.stem:
The team closed its target number of deals this quarter, but revenue is 15 percent below plan. The average deal value fell.
What kind of gap is this?

options.A: A volume gap, so the fix is more calls and more meetings this quarter.
options.B: A conversion gap, so the fix is in how quotes are handled.
options.C: A price gap: deals are closing, but at a lower value than planned.
options.D: No real gap, so lower the revenue target quietly to match the deals.

questions.stem:
One rep's win rate on quotes fell from one in two to one in four. You check the lost quotes: most went out on an old price list, because the new list was never added to the quote templates his branch uses.
What is the gap, and what is the fix?

options.A: A skill gap: role-play quote handling with the rep this week.
options.B: A process gap: get the templates updated, with an owner and a date.
options.C: A capacity gap: move some of the rep's accounts to a colleague.
options.D: A volume gap: ask the rep to send more quotes to make up the difference.

questions.stem:
Before sending a quote, a rep confirmed the client's delivery date, and the client signed the same day.
Which feedback best helps the rep repeat it?

options.A: "Great job on that one!"
options.B: "You're a natural closer. Keep it up."
options.C: "In Tuesday's quote, you confirmed the delivery date before sending, and the client signed that day. Keep doing that."
options.D: Say nothing, because coaching time is for fixing mistakes.

questions.stem:
You are about to join a rep on a client visit for the first time.
What do you tell the rep before you go in?

options.A: "I'm here to check on how you are doing."
options.B: "I'm here to see what works, so we can build on it."
options.C: "If it starts going wrong, I'll take over the meeting."
options.D: Nothing. The rep will see why you are there.

questions.stem:
You asked a rep to "review every key account by month-end." He phoned each one. You meant a full account review with the client, as the team had done before.
What kind of gap is this, and what fixes it?

options.A: A skill gap, fixed with a role-play on running account reviews.
options.B: Persistent underperformance, fixed with a formal conversation.
options.C: A capacity gap, fixed by moving some accounts to a colleague.
options.D: An expectation gap, fixed with a written standard he can repeat back.

questions.stem:
Last week a rep committed in the review to send a revised proposal with phased payments by Friday. The tracker shows it was sent on time. The client is still silent.
What do you do in this week's review?

options.A: Mark it done, then ask whether it worked. If payment terms were not the blocker, find what is before agreeing the next action.
options.B: Mark it done and move on, since the commitment was kept.
options.C: Tell the rep to try harder with the client, since the deal still has not moved.
options.D: Add five new commitments for this deal, so nothing is left untried.

questions.stem:
Leadership asks whether a strategic account will close this quarter. You honestly do not know yet.
What do you say?

options.A: "Yes, it will close," because a decisive answer builds confidence.
options.B: "We will have to wait and see how it goes."
options.C: Give a high figure and pad it a little, so it sounds safe.
options.D: "I don't know yet. We will have a clear answer by the last Friday of the month."

questions.stem:
You have three candidate actions for the next 30 days. Action X would close half the gap, but you are 20 percent confident it will work. Action Y would close a fifth of the gap, at 80 percent confidence. Action Z would close 30 percent of the gap, at 40 percent confidence.
Which do you run first?

options.A: Action X, because it addresses the largest share of the gap.
options.B: Action Y, because it has the largest expected impact.
options.C: Action Z, because it sits in the middle on both measures.
options.D: All three at once, so the gap closes as fast as possible.

questions.stem:
Your 30-day plan aims to cut quote turnaround time. Every faster quote still needs a pricing approval from finance.
When do you involve finance?

options.A: Name the person in finance and walk them through the plan before it starts.
options.B: After the first week, once you have results to show them.
options.C: Only if the plan fails and approvals turn out to be the cause.
options.D: Let each rep contact finance individually when they need an approval.

questions.stem:
Your new segment priority rests on a conversion rate of one in four account reviews. You have never tested that rate. Leadership asks for next quarter's forecast for the segment.
What do you report?

options.A: Present the figure as firm, since leaders prefer confident numbers they can plan with.
options.B: Leave the segment out of the forecast entirely until your own records exist.
options.C: The number and your confidence, the conversion rate labeled as an untested assumption, and what would change the outcome.
options.D: Use the largest market figure you can find, so the segment looks worth the investment.
